entities.name: Preah Vihear Temple
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
Preah Vihear Temple, constructed circa 893 CE, is a prime example of Khmer architecture, located on a 525-meter cliff in Cambodia near the border with Thailand. Its strategic location and architectural grandeur reflect the political and religious aspirations of the Khmer Empire, particularly under the reign of King Yasovarman I. This temple not only served as a significant religious site dedicated to the Hindu god Shiva but also became a focal point of territorial disputes between Cambodia and Thailand, highlighting the complexities of regional nationalism and identity.

The temple complex encompasses a series of sanctuaries linked by pavements and staircases, all oriented toward the north, reflecting the intricate design principles of Khmer architecture. Notably, the temple's construction involved thousands of laborers and artisans, showcasing the Khmer Empire's advanced engineering capabilities. In 1907, the temple was formally recognized as part of Cambodia, yet disputes arose in the 20th century, particularly during the colonial and post-colonial periods, leading to military confrontations and legal battles in international courts. This conflict exemplifies how historical sites can become symbols of national pride and territorial claims.

The legacy of Preah Vihear Temple extends beyond its architectural significance; it has catalyzed a broader discourse on heritage preservation and regional identity. The UNESCO World Heritage designation in 2008 fortified its status as a cultural symbol, reinforcing Cambodia's historical narrative against a backdrop of modern political tensions. The ongoing disputes over the temple have underscored the challenges of post-colonial statehood, where historical claims are intricately woven into contemporary national identities.
